# Multinomial Logistic Regression, Ordinal Regression, and Poisson Regression

> "It's easy to lie with statistics; it is easier to lie without them." - Frederick Mosteller

The previous two chapters were about a response with two categories. This chapter covers three models for responses that are neither binary nor continuous: multinomial logistic regression for unordered categories, ordinal logistic regression for ordered categories, and Poisson regression for counts.

All three are close relatives of binary logistic regression. Each one has a linear predictor $\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}$, a link function that connects the linear predictor to the mean of the response, and coefficients estimated by maximum likelihood. What changes from model to model is the kind of response and, as a result, what the coefficients mean. Most of the mistakes people make with these models come from reading a coefficient as though it came from one of the other models.

## Nominal Response

Logistic regression is most often used when the response has two categories. Sometimes, however, the response has more than two.

If the categories have no natural order, the response is *nominal*. A consumer's choice among product A, product B, and product C is nominal: the categories are names, and there is no sense in which B lies between A and C. Mode of transport to work (car, bus, bicycle, walking), blood type, and political party are other examples.

If the categories do have an order, the response is *ordinal*. Pain rated as none, mild, moderate, or severe is ordinal, and so is a survey answer on a five-point agree/disagree scale. A count, such as the number of store visits, is ordered too, but it is numeric and has no upper limit, so it gets a model of its own.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Nominal, ordinal, and count responses"}

| Response type | Example | Model in this chapter |
|---|---|---|
| Nominal | Product A, product B, product C | Multinomial logistic regression |
| Ordinal | Mild, moderate, severe | Ordinal (proportional odds) logistic regression |
| Count | Number of store visits | Poisson regression |

A nominal model ignores any ordering, an ordinal model uses it, and a Poisson model is for nonnegative integer counts.

:::

Whether a response is nominal or ordinal is sometimes a judgment call. Pregnancy duration grouped into preterm, intermediate, and full term, which is the first example below, is clearly ordered. Hospital discharge status (home, rehabilitation facility, nursing home, died) has a rough order by severity, but whether "rehabilitation facility" is between "home" and "nursing home" for every patient is debatable. When the order is in doubt, fitting both kinds of model and comparing them is reasonable; this chapter does that for the pregnancy data.

## Multinomial Logistic Regression

For a response with $J$ categories, multinomial logistic regression picks one category as the *baseline* and compares each of the other categories with it. If category 1 is the baseline, then for a response with three categories the model is

$$
\log\left(\frac{P(Y=2)}{P(Y=1)}\right)
= \beta_{20}+\beta_{21}x_1+\cdots+\beta_{2,p-1}x_{p-1}
$$

and

$$
\log\left(\frac{P(Y=3)}{P(Y=1)}\right)
= \beta_{30}+\beta_{31}x_1+\cdots+\beta_{3,p-1}x_{p-1}.
$$

Each non-baseline category gets its own intercept and its own slope for every predictor. With $J$ categories and $p-1$ predictors, the model has $(J-1)p$ coefficients. A binary logistic regression is the special case $J=2$.

These equations are called *baseline-category logits*. Solving them for the probabilities gives

$$
P(Y=j)=\frac{\exp(\eta_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^{J}\exp(\eta_k)},
\qquad
\eta_j=\beta_{j0}+\beta_{j1}x_1+\cdots+\beta_{j,p-1}x_{p-1},
$$

with $\eta_1=0$ for the baseline. The denominator makes the $J$ probabilities add to 1, and every probability is between 0 and 1 no matter what values the predictors take.

The comparison between two non-baseline categories is not fitted separately; it follows from the others. Subtracting the two equations above gives

$$
\log\left(\frac{P(Y=3)}{P(Y=2)}\right)
= (\beta_{30}-\beta_{20})+(\beta_{31}-\beta_{21})x_1+\cdots.
$$

So the choice of baseline changes which comparisons are printed, but it does not change the model or its fitted probabilities.

:::: {#exm-25_1 .example title="Pregnancy duration data"}

A study was undertaken to examine the association between several risk factors and pregnancy duration.

The response variable has three categories:

| Code | Pregnancy duration category |
|---:|---|
| 1 | Preterm: less than 36 weeks |
| 2 | Intermediate: 36 to 37 weeks |
| 3 | Full term: 38 weeks or greater |

The predictors are:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $X_1$ | Nutritional status; higher scores indicate better nutritional status |
| $X_2$ | Indicator for age less than or equal to 20 |
| $X_3$ | Indicator for age greater than 30 |
| $X_4$ | Indicator for alcohol history |
| $X_5$ | Indicator for smoking history |

The age categories are represented by two indicator variables:

| Age category | $X_2$ | $X_3$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| Less than or equal to 20 | 1 | 0 |
| 21 to 30 | 0 | 0 |
| Greater than 30 | 0 | 1 |

Thus, age 21 to 30 is the reference group.

::::

:::: {#exm-25_2 .example title="Loading and preparing the pregnancy data"}

We read the data, name the variables, and convert the response to a factor. The data file also contains three indicator columns for the response categories, which we drop because the factor `Y` carries the same information.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(poissonreg)

tidymodels_prefer()

pregnancy_data <- read.table("CH14TA13.txt")

names(pregnancy_data) <- c(
  "id", "Y", "Y1", "Y2", "Y3",
  "X1", "X2", "X3", "X4", "X5"
)

pregnancy_data <- pregnancy_data |>
  mutate(
    Y = factor(
      Y,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Preterm", "Intermediate", "FullTerm")
    )
  ) |>
  select(-id, -Y1, -Y2, -Y3)

pregnancy_data |>
  count(Y) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             Y  n proportion
1      Preterm 26  0.2549020
2 Intermediate 35  0.3431373
3     FullTerm 41  0.4019608
```


:::
:::


There are 102 pregnancies. The smallest category, `Preterm`, has 26. That number limits how many coefficients the data can support: the multinomial model below has 12 coefficients, and half of them are estimated from the contrast between `FullTerm` and only 26 preterm cases.

A few targeted plots are easier to read than a large scatterplot matrix. We start with the distribution of the response categories.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
duration_colors <- c(
  Preterm = "#D55E00",
  Intermediate = "#E69F00",
  FullTerm = "#0072B2"
)

pregnancy_data |>
  count(Y) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Y, y = n, fill = Y)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = duration_colors) +
  labs(
    x = "Pregnancy duration category",
    y = "Number of observations",
    title = "Pregnancy duration category counts"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](25_Multinomial_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='Bar chart showing the number of observations in each pregnancy duration category: 26 preterm, 35 intermediate, and 41 full term.' width=576}
:::
:::


Next, we look at nutritional status by pregnancy duration category.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pregnancy_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Y, y = X1, color = Y)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = duration_colors) +
  labs(
    x = "Pregnancy duration category",
    y = "Nutritional status",
    color = "Category",
    title = "Nutritional status by pregnancy duration"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](25_Multinomial_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-alt='Boxplots and jittered points showing nutritional status by pregnancy duration category. Median nutritional status is higher in the full-term group than in the other two groups.' width=576}
:::
:::


The full-term group has higher nutritional scores on the whole, while the preterm and intermediate groups look similar. A plot like this already suggests that the effect of nutrition may not be the same for every comparison between categories, which is something a multinomial model allows and an ordinal model does not.

Finally, we look at the observed category proportions for each indicator predictor.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pregnancy_indicator_proportions <- pregnancy_data |>
  select(Y, X2, X3, X4, X5) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = X2:X5,
    names_to = "predictor",
    values_to = "indicator_value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    predictor = recode(
      predictor,
      X2 = "Age <= 20",
      X3 = "Age > 30",
      X4 = "Alcohol history",
      X5 = "Smoking history"
    ),
    indicator_value = factor(indicator_value, levels = c(0, 1))
  ) |>
  count(predictor, indicator_value, Y) |>
  group_by(predictor, indicator_value) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

pregnancy_indicator_proportions |>
  ggplot(aes(x = indicator_value, y = proportion, fill = Y)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ predictor) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = duration_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(
    x = "Indicator value",
    y = "Observed category proportion",
    fill = "Category",
    title = "Pregnancy duration proportions by indicator value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](25_Multinomial_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='Faceted stacked bar charts showing observed pregnancy duration proportions for indicator values 0 and 1 of four binary predictors. The full-term share is smaller when the indicator is 1 for every predictor.' width=576}
:::
:::


For each of the four indicators, the full-term share is smaller in the group coded 1. These are unadjusted comparisons. The age indicators and the behavior indicators may be related to each other and to nutrition, so the model is needed to separate them.

::::

:::: {#exm-25_3 .example title="Fitting a multinomial logistic regression model"}

We fit the model with a `tidymodels` workflow. The `nnet` engine fits the model by maximum likelihood.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pregnancy_recipe <- recipe(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5, data = pregnancy_data)

pregnancy_model <- multinom_reg() |>
  set_engine("nnet")

pregnancy_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(pregnancy_recipe) |>
  add_model(pregnancy_model)

pregnancy_fit <- pregnancy_workflow |>
  fit(data = pregnancy_data)
```
:::


The first level of the factor, `Preterm`, is the baseline. The model fits one equation for `Intermediate` versus `Preterm` and another for `FullTerm` versus `Preterm`. The coefficients are on the log-odds scale, one row per non-baseline category.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pregnancy_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  coef()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             (Intercept)         X1          X2         X3         X4
Intermediate   -1.517009 0.01897219 -0.04355881 -0.1721573 -0.9758857
FullTerm       -5.475353 0.06542052 -2.95693397 -2.0596355 -2.0428964
                     X5
Intermediate -0.2218629
FullTerm     -2.4522828
```


:::
:::


`tidy()` gives the same coefficients in long form with standard errors, Wald $z$ statistics, and confidence intervals. With `exponentiate = TRUE`, the estimates and intervals are odds ratios.

There is a catch. To get standard errors, the `tidy()` method for `multinom` fits calls `summary()`, which refits the model using the data named in the original call. Inside a workflow, that data is not available under its original name, and `tidy(pregnancy_fit)` stops with the error "'data' must be a data.frame, environment, or list". The fix is to fit the same model with `nnet::multinom()` directly. We will need this fit for the likelihood ratio tests below as well.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(nnet)

full_multinom <- multinom(
  Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5,
  data = pregnancy_data,
  trace = FALSE
)

all.equal(coef(full_multinom), coef(extract_fit_engine(pregnancy_fit)), tolerance = 1e-4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
pregnancy_or <- full_multinom |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

pregnancy_or |>
  select(y.level, term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  print(n = Inf)
```

Here is how to read a few of these, holding the other predictors fixed.

The `X1` coefficient in the `FullTerm` row is about 0.065, so each one-point increase in nutritional status multiplies the odds of a full-term birth rather than a preterm birth by about $\exp(0.065)=1.07$. Over a 10-point difference, which is less than the spread between the quartiles of $X_1$ (about 121 to 149), the factor is $\exp(0.65)\approx 1.9$.

The `X5` (smoking) odds ratio in the `FullTerm` row is about 0.09: smokers have roughly one-twelfth the odds of a full-term birth rather than a preterm birth.

In the `Intermediate` row, every interval contains 1; the smallest $p$-value, about 0.10, is for alcohol history. The data say little about what separates intermediate from preterm pregnancies. Most of the signal is in the comparison of full-term with preterm.

The odds ratios are for pairs of categories. "Smoking multiplies the odds of a full-term birth by 0.09" is not correct as it stands, because the comparison category, preterm, is part of the statement. The odds of full term versus *not* full term would require a different model.

::::

:::: {#exm-25_baseline .example title="Changing the baseline category"}

Comparing `FullTerm` with `Intermediate` is not printed above, but it is part of the model. One way to see it is to subtract rows. For smoking, the log odds ratio for full term versus intermediate is $-2.452-(-0.222)=-2.230$.

The other way is to refit the model with a different baseline. `fct_relevel()` moves `FullTerm` to the first level. The recipe records the factor levels of the data it was created with, so reusing `pregnancy_workflow` on the releveled data stops with an error about mismatched factor levels. We build a new recipe from the releveled data instead.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pregnancy_data_fullterm <- pregnancy_data |>
  mutate(Y = fct_relevel(Y, "FullTerm"))

pregnancy_fit_fullterm <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(recipe(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5, data = pregnancy_data_fullterm)) |>
  add_model(pregnancy_model) |>
  fit(data = pregnancy_data_fullterm)

pregnancy_fit_fullterm |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  coef()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             (Intercept)          X1       X2       X3       X4       X5
Preterm         5.475147 -0.06541919 2.957028 2.059662 2.042900 2.452362
Intermediate    3.958370 -0.04644903 2.913475 1.887550 1.067001 2.230492
```


:::
:::


The `Intermediate` row is now intermediate versus full term. Its `X5` coefficient, about 2.23, is the negative of the difference we computed, as it should be. The `Preterm` row is the old `FullTerm` row with every sign reversed.

The fitted probabilities are the same in both fits, up to the convergence tolerance of the optimizer.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
probs_preterm_base <- predict(pregnancy_fit, pregnancy_data, type = "prob")
probs_fullterm_base <- predict(pregnancy_fit_fullterm, pregnancy_data, type = "prob")

max(abs(
  as.matrix(probs_preterm_base) -
    as.matrix(probs_fullterm_base[, names(probs_preterm_base)])
))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1.777432e-05
```


:::
:::


The choice of baseline is a choice of which comparisons to report. A good baseline is a category that readers naturally compare against (a control group, the most common outcome, or the "normal" outcome) and one that has a reasonable number of observations. A rare baseline category makes every coefficient's standard error large, because every comparison involves it.

::::

### Testing a Predictor in a Multinomial Model

Each predictor in a multinomial model has $J-1$ coefficients, one per non-baseline category. The question "does smoking history matter?" is a question about all of them at once, so the test has $J-1$ degrees of freedom. The likelihood ratio test from the previous chapter works the same way: fit the model with and without the predictor and compare the deviances.

:::: {#exm-25_mnlrt .example title="Likelihood ratio tests for the multinomial model"}

We fit the models with `nnet::multinom()` directly. As in @exm-24_lrt, `anova()` should be given ordinary model fits rather than the engine fit extracted from a workflow.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
no_smoking_multinom <- multinom(
  Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4,
  data = pregnancy_data,
  trace = FALSE
)

anova(no_smoking_multinom, full_multinom)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Likelihood ratio tests of Multinomial Models

1      X1 + X2 + X3 + X4       194   186.1517                      
2 X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5       192   168.6754 1 vs 2     2 17.47627
       Pr(Chi)
1

```


:::
:::


The deviance drops by about 17.5 on 2 degrees of freedom when smoking history is added, which is strong evidence that smoking is associated with pregnancy duration.

To test each predictor in turn, we loop over the predictors and drop one at a time.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
predictors <- c("X1", "X2", "X3", "X4", "X5")

map(predictors, \(v) {
  reduced <- multinom(
    reformulate(setdiff(predictors, v), response = "Y"),
    data = pregnancy_data,
    trace = FALSE
  )
  tibble(
    dropped = v,
    lr_statistic = deviance(reduced) - deviance(full_multinom),
    df = 2,
    p_value = pchisq(lr_statistic, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
  )
}) |>
  list_rbind()
```

The two age indicators together describe one variable, age group. A test of whether age group matters drops $X_2$ and $X_3$ together, for $2 \times 2 = 4$ degrees of freedom.


::: {.cell}

### Seeing the Model on the Probability Scale

A table of 12 odds ratios is hard to take in. Plotting fitted probabilities against a predictor, with the other predictors held at chosen values, usually communicates the model better.

:::: {#exm-25_mneffect .example title="Fitted category probabilities against nutritional status"}

We predict on a grid of nutritional scores for a 21- to 30-year-old with no alcohol history, once for a nonsmoker and once for a smoker.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nutrition_grid <- crossing(
  X1 = seq(95, 195, by = 1),
  X5 = c(0, 1)
) |>
  mutate(X2 = 0, X3 = 0, X4 = 0)

nutrition_probs <- nutrition_grid |>
  bind_cols(predict(pregnancy_fit, new_data = nutrition_grid, type = "prob")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with(".pred_"),
    names_to = "category",
    names_prefix = ".pred_",
    values_to = "probability"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    category = factor(category, levels = c("Preterm", "Intermediate", "FullTerm")),
    smoking = if_else(X5 == 1, "Smoker", "Nonsmoker")
  )

nutrition_probs |>
  ggplot(aes(x = X1, y = probability, color = category)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ smoking) +
  scale_color_manual(values = duration_colors) +
  labs(
    x = "Nutritional status",
    y = "Fitted probability",
    color = "Category",
    title = "Fitted category probabilities, age 21 to 30, no alcohol history"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](25_Multinomial_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-alt='Two panels of fitted probabilities against nutritional status for a nonsmoker and a smoker. The full-term probability rises with nutritional status in both panels and is lower for the smoker. The intermediate probability falls for the nonsmoker and rises and then falls for the smoker.' width=576}
:::
:::


For a nonsmoker, the full-term probability rises from about 0.47 at a nutritional score of 95 to 0.99 at 195, and the intermediate probability falls from about 0.30 to almost 0. For a smoker, the intermediate curve is not monotone: it rises to about 0.49 near a score of 107, as preterm births become less likely, and then falls as full-term births take over.

This is a general feature of multinomial models. Every coefficient for `Intermediate` in @exm-25_3 is a comparison with `Preterm`, and the `X1` coefficient for `Intermediate` is positive, yet the probability of an intermediate birth goes *down* as $X_1$ increases (for a nonsmoker, over the whole range plotted). The sign of a baseline-category coefficient tells you the direction of one odds ratio, not the direction in which that category's probability moves. That direction depends on all of the categories at once.

### Predictions and Evaluation

:::: {#exm-25_4 .example title="Predicted probabilities and classes from a multinomial model"}

A multinomial model gives one predicted probability for each response category. A common classification rule is to predict the category with the largest fitted probability.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pregnancy_predictions <- pregnancy_data |>
  select(Y) |>
  bind_cols(
    predict(pregnancy_fit, new_data = pregnancy_data, type = "prob"),
    predict(pregnancy_fit, new_data = pregnancy_data, type = "class")
  )

pregnancy_predictions |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false" title="Independence of irrelevant alternatives"}

The multinomial logit model implies that the odds of choosing category $A$ over category $B$ do not depend on what other categories are available. This property is called the *independence of irrelevant alternatives* (IIA).

It is unrealistic when two categories are close substitutes. In the standard example, commuters choose between a car and a red bus with probability 1/2 each. Adding a blue bus that is identical to the red bus should split the bus riders, leaving car 1/2, red bus 1/4, blue bus 1/4. The multinomial logit model instead keeps the car-to-red-bus odds at 1 and gives each option 1/3.

IIA matters most for choice data, such as product or travel-mode choice, and when one wants to predict what happens if an option is added or removed. For outcomes like pregnancy duration, where the categories are fixed intervals of one quantity, it is rarely a concern.

:::

## Ordinal Regression

### Ordinal Response

When the response categories have a meaningful order, the response is *ordinal*. Pregnancy duration can be treated as ordinal because

$$
\text{Preterm} < \text{Intermediate} < \text{FullTerm}.
$$

Multinomial logistic regression can still be used, but it ignores the ordering. Ordinal logistic regression uses it. The most common ordinal model is the *proportional odds model*, which models cumulative probabilities

$$
P(Y_i \le j), \qquad j=1,\ldots,J-1,
$$

rather than the probabilities $P(Y_i=j)$ of single categories. For pregnancy duration, the two cumulative probabilities are $P(Y_i\le\text{Preterm})$ and $P(Y_i\le\text{Intermediate})$. The third, $P(Y_i\le\text{FullTerm})$, is always 1.

The model puts each cumulative probability on the logit scale. In the parameterization used by `MASS::polr()`,

$$
\log\left(\frac{P(Y_i\le j)}{P(Y_i> j)}\right)=\zeta_j-\eta_i,
\qquad
\eta_i=\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_{p-1}x_{i,p-1}.
$$

The $\zeta_j$ are *cutpoints*, one for each of the $J-1$ boundaries between adjacent categories, with $\zeta_1<\zeta_2<\cdots<\zeta_{J-1}$. The linear predictor $\eta_i$ has no intercept, because the cutpoints play that role.

Because $\eta_i$ is subtracted, a positive $\beta_k$ makes the cumulative probabilities smaller and so moves probability toward the *higher* categories. Some software (SAS, and some R packages) writes the model as $\zeta_j+\eta_i$ instead, which reverses every sign. Before interpreting an ordinal model's coefficients, check which form the software uses.

The probability of a single category is a difference of cumulative probabilities:

$$
P(Y_i=j)=P(Y_i\le j)-P(Y_i\le j-1).
$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Why use an ordinal model?"}

The proportional odds model is more parsimonious. It has one slope per predictor plus $J-1$ cutpoints, while the multinomial model has $J-1$ slopes per predictor. For the pregnancy data, that is 7 parameters instead of 12. With more categories the savings grow: a five-category response with five predictors needs 9 parameters in the ordinal model and 24 in the multinomial model.

Fewer parameters mean smaller standard errors when the model is right. The price is a stronger assumption, described next.

:::

### A Latent-Variable View

A useful way to think about the proportional odds model is that there is an unobserved continuous variable behind the categories. For pregnancy duration, that variable could be the length of the pregnancy itself, which we observe only after it has been grouped into three bins.

Suppose

$$
Y_i^* = \eta_i + \varepsilon_i,
$$

where $\varepsilon_i$ has a standard logistic distribution, and we observe category $j$ when $Y_i^*$ falls between $\zeta_{j-1}$ and $\zeta_j$. Then $P(Y_i\le j)=P(Y_i^*\le\zeta_j)=F(\zeta_j-\eta_i)$, where $F$ is the logistic CDF. That is exactly the model above.

In this picture, changing the predictors slides the whole distribution of $Y^*$ left or right, while the cutpoints stay put.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

latent_curves <- crossing(

  eta = c(3, 5)
) |>
  mutate(
    density = dlogis(y_star, location = eta),
    eta_label = paste("Linear predictor =", eta)
  )

latent_curves |>
  ggplot(aes(x = y_star, y = density, color = eta_label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cutpoints, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.27, label = "Preterm") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.98, y = 0.27, label = "Intermediate") +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = 0.27, label = "FullTerm") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2")) +
  labs(

    y = "Density",
    color = NULL,
    title = "Shifting the latent distribution past fixed cutpoints"
```

### Proportional Odds Assumption

The proportional odds model assumes that each predictor has the same effect at every cumulative split of the ordered response. For the pregnancy duration categories, the splits are:

| Split | Comparison |
|---|---|
| 1 | Preterm versus Intermediate or FullTerm |
| 2 | Preterm or Intermediate versus FullTerm |

The cutpoints differ from split to split, but the slopes are shared. On the cumulative logit scale, the curves for the two splits are parallel, which is why the assumption is also called the *parallel slopes* assumption. The name "proportional odds" comes from the fact that, for two people with linear predictors $\eta_a$ and $\eta_b$, the ratio of their cumulative odds is $\exp(\eta_b-\eta_a)$ at every split.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false" title="When the assumption may be questionable"}

The proportional odds assumption may fail if a predictor affects one boundary much more than another.

For example, if smoking history strongly separates `Preterm` from the other categories but has little relationship to whether a pregnancy is `FullTerm`, then one shared slope is too restrictive. In that case, a multinomial model or a more flexible ordinal model (a partial proportional odds model, which lets some predictors have split-specific slopes) may be more appropriate.

:::

:::: {#exm-25_5 .example title="Fitting a proportional odds model"}

## Poisson Regression

Poisson regression is used when the response is a count:

$$
Y_i = 0,1,2,\ldots
$$

Examples include the number of store visits, hospitalizations, manufacturing defects, insurance claims, or accidents at an intersection, each counted over some fixed period or area.

### The Poisson Distribution

The Poisson probability distribution is

$$
f(Y) = \frac{\mu^Y \exp(-\mu)}{Y!}, \qquad Y=0,1,2,\ldots
$$

For a Poisson random variable,

$$
\begin{align*}
E(Y) &= \mu,\\
Var(Y) &= \mu.
\end{align*}
$$

The mean and the variance are the same. A Poisson model has no separate variance parameter like $\sigma^2$ in linear regression: once the mean is known, so is the variance. This is the assumption that most often fails in practice, and we return to it below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
    mu_label = factor(paste("Mean =", mu), levels = paste("Mean =", c(1, 4, 10)))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = y, y = probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  facet_wrap(~ mu_label) +
  labs(
    x = "Count",
    y = "Probability",
    title = "Poisson distributions with different means"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

When the mean is small, the distribution is piled up near zero and skewed to the right. As the mean grows, it spreads out (its standard deviation is $\sqrt{\mu}$) and becomes more symmetric. A linear model with constant variance cannot describe both shapes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="Counts are not just another continuous response"}

A count is nonnegative and discrete, and its variance tends to grow with its mean. A linear model can predict negative counts, and it assumes the same variance everywhere. A Poisson model with a log link keeps the fitted mean positive and lets the variance grow with the mean.

Transforming the response, for example fitting a linear model to $\log(Y+1)$, is a common workaround. It handles skewness somewhat, but the constant added before taking logs is arbitrary, the coefficients describe the mean of $\log(Y+1)$ rather than the mean count, and it behaves poorly when many counts are 0 or 1.

:::

### Poisson Regression Model

In Poisson regression, we assume

$$
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i)
$$

and use the log link

$$
\log(\mu_i)=\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\mu_i=\exp(\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}).
$$

This guarantees that the fitted mean count is positive. It also makes the predictors act multiplicatively. A one-unit increase in $x_k$ adds $\beta_k$ to $\log(\mu_i)$, which multiplies $\mu_i$ by $\exp(\beta_k)$. So $\exp(\beta_k)$ is a *rate ratio*: the factor by which the expected count changes per unit of $x_k$, holding the other predictors fixed. A rate ratio of 1.18 means an 18% increase in the expected count, and 0.88 means a 12% decrease.

As with logistic regression, the coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood, the fit is summarized by the deviance, and nested models are compared with likelihood ratio tests.

### Checking the Fit

A Poisson model can go wrong in a few specific ways: the variance can be larger than the mean (overdispersion), there can be more zeros than the model expects, or the log of the mean can depend on a predictor in a way that is not linear. Each one has a direct check.

:::: {#exm-25_dispersion .example title="Checking for overdispersion"}

If the Poisson model is right, the Pearson residuals

$$
r_i=\frac{Y_i-\hat{\mu}_i}{\sqrt{\hat{\mu}_i}}
$$

have variance about 1. The sum of their squares divided by the residual degrees of freedom estimates the *dispersion*, which should be close to 1. A value well above 1 is *overdispersion*.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(
  pearson_dispersion = sum(residuals(lumber_glm, type = "pearson")^2) /
    df.residual(lumber_glm),
  residual_deviance = deviance(lumber_glm),
  df = df.residual(lumber_glm),
  goodness_of_fit_p = pchisq(residual_deviance, df, lower.tail = FALSE)
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

               <dbl>             <dbl> <int>             <dbl>
1              0.980              115.   104             0.217
```


:::
:::


The dispersion estimate is about 0.98, and the residual deviance, about 115 on 104 degrees of freedom, is consistent with the Poisson model (the goodness-of-fit $p$-value is about 0.22). Once the predictors are taken into account, the counts vary about as much as a Poisson model says they should. The marginal variance of 44 in @exm-25_7 came from differences between the tracts' means.

The deviance goodness-of-fit test needs fairly large fitted counts to be trustworthy. The smallest fitted mean here is about 4, which is adequate. When many fitted means are below 1 or 2, the deviance does not follow a $\chi^2$ distribution well and the test should not be relied on.

A plot of Pearson residuals against fitted values shows the same thing graphically: no funnel shape, and all but 8 of the 110 residuals between $-2$ and 2, close to the 5% one would expect by chance. The largest is about 2.5.

:::: {#exm-25_quasi .example title="What overdispersion does to inference"}

The lumber data are not overdispersed, so we simulate data that are. We generate counts from a negative binomial distribution, whose variance is $\mu+\mu^2/\theta$, larger than its mean. With $\theta=2$ and means around 3 to 4, the variance is roughly three times the mean. We fit an ordinary Poisson model and a quasi-Poisson model to each of 1,000 simulated datasets and record whether the 95% confidence interval for the slope contains the true value, 0.5.

The quasi-Poisson model has the same coefficient estimates as the Poisson model but multiplies the standard errors by the square root of the estimated dispersion.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(3386)

n_obs <- 100
x_sim <- runif(n_obs)
true_slope <- 0.5

overdispersion_sim <- map(1:1000, \(rep) {
  y_sim <- rnbinom(n_obs, mu = exp(1 + true_slope * x_sim), size = 2)

  poisson_fit <- glm(y_sim ~ x_sim, family = poisson)
  quasi_fit <- glm(y_sim ~ x_sim, family = quasipoisson)

  bind_rows(
    tidy(poisson_fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.method = "Wald") |>
      mutate(model = "Poisson"),
    tidy(quasi_fit) |>
      mutate(
        conf.low = estimate - qt(0.975, n_obs - 2) * std.error,
        conf.high = estimate + qt(0.975, n_obs - 2) * std.error,
        model = "Quasi-Poisson"
      )
  ) |>
    filter(term == "x_sim") |>
    mutate(
      rep = rep,
      dispersion = sum(residuals(poisson_fit, type = "pearson")^2) / (n_obs - 2)
    )
}) |>
  list_rbind()

overdispersion_sim |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(
    mean_std_error = mean(std.error),
    coverage = mean(conf.low <= true_slope & true_slope <= conf.high),
    mean_dispersion = mean(dispersion)
  )
```

The coefficient estimates themselves are the same in both models and are unbiased; the problem is entirely in the standard errors, and so in every test and interval.

### Exposure and Offsets

Counts often come from units of different sizes or observed for different lengths of time: accidents at intersections with different traffic volumes, infections among hospitals with different numbers of patient-days, customers from census tracts with different numbers of households. Then the natural quantity to model is a *rate*, the count per unit of exposure $t_i$:

$$
\log\left(\frac{\mu_i}{t_i}\right)=\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\log(\mu_i)=\log(t_i)+\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

The term $\log(t_i)$ is an *offset*: a predictor whose coefficient is fixed at 1 rather than estimated. It says that doubling the exposure doubles the expected count, all else equal. In R, it goes in the formula as `offset(log(t))`.

An offset is an assumption, and it can be checked by putting $\log(t_i)$ in the model as an ordinary predictor and seeing whether its coefficient is near 1.

:::: {#exm-25_offset .example title="Should housing units be an offset?"}

It seems natural to treat the number of housing units in a tract, $X_1$, as exposure: a tract with twice as many households might be expected to send twice as many customers. We fit the model with $\log(X_1)$ as an offset and with $\log(X_1)$ as an estimated predictor.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lumber_offset <- glm(
  Y ~ offset(log(X1)) + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5,
  data = lumber_data,
  family = poisson
)

lumber_log_units <- glm(
  Y ~ log(X1) + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5,
  data = lumber_data,
  family = poisson
)

tidy(lumber_log_units, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "log(X1)") |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
```

## Things to Watch Out For

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false" title="Common mistakes with multinomial, ordinal, and Poisson models"}

- Reading a multinomial coefficient without its comparison category. Every coefficient compares a category with the baseline; say which two categories are being compared.
- Reading the sign of a multinomial coefficient as the direction in which that category's probability moves. The probability of a middle category can fall even when its coefficient is positive (@exm-25_mneffect).
- Using a rare category as the multinomial baseline, which inflates the standard errors of every coefficient.
- Testing a multinomial predictor one coefficient at a time. A predictor has $J-1$ coefficients, and the test of the predictor has $J-1$ degrees of freedom (@exm-25_mnlrt).
- Fitting too many coefficients for the size of the smallest category. With 26 preterm births, the pregnancy data support only a handful of predictors in a multinomial model.
- Letting R choose the order of an ordinal response. Alphabetical order can reverse or scramble the categories without a warning (@exm-25_wrongorder).
- Interpreting `polr()` coefficients with the sign convention of another program. `polr()` uses $\zeta_j-\eta_i$, so positive coefficients mean higher categories.
- Taking a nonsignificant check of the proportional odds assumption as proof that it holds. With small samples, the check has little power (@exm-25_pocheck).
- Treating ordinal codes 1, 2, 3 as a numeric response in a linear model. That assumes the categories are equally spaced, which the data cannot confirm.
- Judging overdispersion from the raw mean and variance of the counts. The assumption is about the variance given the predictors (@exm-25_dispersion).
- Ignoring overdispersion. The coefficients are fine, but standard errors, tests, and intervals are all too optimistic (@exm-25_quasi).
- Using an offset without checking that the count is proportional to the exposure (@exm-25_offset).
- Fitting a linear model to counts, or to $\log(Y+1)$, when many counts are small.
- Extrapolating a log-linear model. Predicted counts grow or shrink exponentially outside the range of the data.

:::

## Recap

This chapter introduced three regression models for categorical and count responses.

| Idea | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Nominal response | A categorical response whose categories have no natural order. |
| Multinomial logistic regression | A model for nominal responses with more than two categories. |
| Baseline category | The category every other category is compared with in a multinomial model. Changing it changes the printed comparisons but not the fitted probabilities. |
| Category-specific coefficients | Separate coefficients for each non-baseline category comparison, $(J-1)p$ in all. |
| Multinomial predicted probabilities | One fitted probability for each response category, adding to 1. |
| Multinomial log loss | A metric that evaluates the predicted probability of the category that occurred. |
| Independence of irrelevant alternatives | The multinomial logit property that the odds of one category over another do not depend on the other categories. |
| Ordinal response | A categorical response whose categories have a meaningful order. |
| Proportional odds model | An ordinal logistic model for cumulative probabilities, with shared slopes and separate cutpoints. |
| Cutpoints | Thresholds that separate adjacent ordered categories on the logit scale. |
| Latent variable | An unobserved continuous variable whose position relative to the cutpoints determines the observed category. |
| Proportional odds assumption | The assumption that each predictor's effect is the same at every cumulative split; also called parallel slopes. |
| Count response | A nonnegative integer response variable. |
| Poisson distribution | A count distribution whose mean and variance are both $\mu$. |
| Poisson regression | A regression model for counts with a log link, $\log(\mu_i)=\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}$. |
| Rate ratio | The exponentiated Poisson coefficient: the factor by which the expected count is multiplied per unit increase in the predictor. |
| Overdispersion | Variance larger than the Poisson model allows, given the predictors. It makes Poisson standard errors too small. |
| Quasi-Poisson and negative binomial models | Two ways to allow for overdispersion. |
| Offset | A term with its coefficient fixed at 1, used to model counts per unit of exposure. |
| Observed versus expected frequencies | A comparison of how often each count occurs with how often the model predicts it, which can reveal excess zeros. |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

1. Nominal categories have no natural order; ordinal categories do. Favorite music genre is nominal; letter grade (A through F) is ordinal.

2. The multinomial model has $(4-1)(3+1)=12$ coefficients. The proportional odds model has 3 slopes and 3 cutpoints, 6 parameters in all.

3. Each coefficient row compares one of the other categories with preterm. The `Intermediate` row is about the odds of intermediate rather than preterm, and the `FullTerm` row is about the odds of full term rather than preterm.

4. The log odds ratio is $-2.452-(-0.222)=-2.230$, so the odds ratio is $\exp(-2.230)\approx 0.11$. Smokers have about one-ninth the odds of a full-term rather than an intermediate birth.

5. The coefficients change, because they now describe comparisons with a different category, but they are linear combinations of the old ones. The fitted probabilities do not change.

6. Every comparison involves the baseline. If the baseline has few observations, every coefficient is estimated imprecisely.

7. Four. The predictor has one coefficient for each of the $5-1=4$ non-baseline categories, and the test asks whether all four are zero.

8. The coefficient describes the odds of intermediate relative to preterm, and that ratio does increase with nutrition. But full-term births increase faster, so at high nutritional scores probability moves from intermediate to full term, and the probability of intermediate falls.

9. The model's accuracy has to be compared with what is possible without predictors. Always predicting the largest category, `FullTerm`, is right 40% of the time, so the model's 66% has to be judged against 40%, not 0% or 33%.

10. Accuracy uses only the predicted class. Log loss uses the predicted probability of the category that occurred, so it distinguishes a confident correct prediction from a lucky guess and penalizes confident mistakes heavily.

11. The odds of choosing one category over another do not depend on which other categories exist. It matters when categories can be substitutes for each other, as in choices among products or modes of transport. Pregnancy duration categories are intervals of one quantity, not alternatives a person chooses among, so the property means little there.

12. It uses the order. It has fewer parameters, so its estimates are more precise when its assumption holds, and its coefficients have a single interpretation in terms of higher versus lower categories.

13. They are probabilities of being at or below a category, such as $P(Y\le\text{Intermediate})$. A single category's probability is a difference of adjacent cumulative probabilities, $P(Y=j)=P(Y\le j)-P(Y\le j-1)$.

14. Toward higher categories. A larger $\eta_i$ makes $\zeta_j-\eta_i$ smaller and so makes every cumulative probability $P(Y\le j)$ smaller.

15. $\exp(-1.59)\approx 0.20$. At either split, smokers have about 0.20 times the odds of nonsmokers of being in a longer duration category, holding the other predictors fixed. Equivalently, smokers' odds of a shorter duration category are about 4.9 times as large.

16. An unobserved continuous variable $Y^*=\eta_i+\varepsilon_i$ determines the category: the observed category is whichever interval between cutpoints $Y^*$ falls into. A change in a predictor shifts the distribution of $Y^*$; the cutpoints and the shape of the distribution stay fixed.

17. It says each predictor has the same slope at every cumulative split. One check fits a binary logistic regression for each split, such as preterm versus the rest and full term versus the rest, and compares the slopes. Similar slopes support the assumption.

18. The slopes have standard errors of about 0.5 to 0.6, and their intervals overlap widely. With 102 observations, the difference could be sampling variation. The check has little power, so it cannot show that the assumption holds either.

19. The two models are not nested: the proportional odds model is not obtained by setting some multinomial coefficients to zero. AIC was used instead. The proportional odds model had the lower AIC, about 187.5 compared with 192.7.

20. The levels are placed in alphabetical order. For the pregnancy data, that reverses the true order and flips the sign of every coefficient; for other labels it can scramble the categories. No warning is given.

21. The log link keeps the expected count positive. Because $\mu_i=\exp(\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta})$, each predictor multiplies the expected count by $\exp(\beta_k)$ per unit, so effects are multiplicative.

22. $0.879^3\approx 0.68$, a decrease of about 32% in the expected count.

23. The Poisson assumption concerns the variance of $Y$ given the predictors. Tracts have different means, so the unconditional variance is larger than the unconditional mean even if each tract's count is Poisson. The check is the Pearson dispersion statistic from the fitted model, which was about 0.98.

24. Overdispersion is variance larger than the mean, given the predictors. The coefficient estimates are still consistent, but the standard errors are too small, so tests reject too often and confidence intervals are too narrow. In the simulation, nominal 95% intervals covered the true slope only about 77% of the time.

25. An offset is a term in the linear predictor with its coefficient fixed at 1. The log of exposure is used as an offset when the count should be proportional to exposure, for example when units are observed for different lengths of time. To check it, put the log of exposure in as an ordinary predictor and see whether its coefficient is close to 1. For the lumber data it was about 0.20, so housing units should not be an offset.

26. All three zero tracts were more than 9 miles from the store and close to a competitor, so customers beyond some distance may stop coming altogether, which a smooth exponential decline does not capture. A more flexible term for distance, or a zero-inflated Poisson model, could address it.

27. They are designed for different kinds of response, and their coefficients mean different things. Multinomial coefficients compare pairs of categories, ordinal coefficients describe shifts toward higher categories, and Poisson coefficients describe multiplicative changes in an expected count. Using the wrong model gives coefficients that answer the wrong question.
